message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) Below is a concise overview of the key protections and responsibilities that apply to residential tenants in Texas. These rights are derived from state statutes (primarily the Texas Property Code), local ordinances, and federal law. For specific situations—especially those involving disputes, evictions, or health & safety concerns—consult a qualified attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization. | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may charge a **maximum of one month’s rent** for a security deposit.
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a written move‑in checklist.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the deposit is withheld. | | **Habitability / Repairs** | • Landlords must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control).
• The landlord must repair any major defects within a reasonable time after notice. | • Provide written notice (email or certified mail) of needed repairs.
• If the landlord fails to act, you may file a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) or seek a court order. | | **Rent Payment & Late Fees** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Landlords may charge a **late fee** only if it is stated in the lease and is **reasonable** (not punitive). | • Pay on time; if late, negotiate a payment plan. | | **Privacy & Entry** | • Landlords must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24–48 hrs) before entering, except in emergencies.
• Entry is allowed for inspections, repairs, or showing the unit to prospective tenants. | • Keep a log of all entries.
• If you suspect unlawful entry, document the incident and consider filing a complaint. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on **race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, or source of income** (e.g., public assistance). | • File a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR). | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party may terminate a lease with **proper notice** (typically 30 days for month‑to‑month).
• Landlords must provide a **written notice** of termination. | • Keep copies of all notices. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the **Texas Eviction Law**: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment, 30‑day notice for lease violation).
• If the landlord files an eviction suit, you have the right to contest it in court. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• Attend all court hearings; bring evidence (e.g., receipts, repair requests). | | **Health & Safety** | • Landlords must comply with local building codes, fire safety regulations, and the Texas Health and Safety Code. | • Report violations to local health or building departments. | | **Utilities** | • Landlords may require you to pay utilities unless otherwise specified. | • Verify utility responsibilities in the lease. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • You may sublet or assign the lease only with the landlord’s **written consent** (unless the lease prohibits it). | • Obtain written permission before moving a tenant in. | | **Right to Counsel** | • In eviction proceedings, you have the right to be represented by an attorney or a tenant‑rights organization. | • Seek legal aid if you cannot afford counsel. | --- #### Quick Steps If You Encounter a Problem 1. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written correspondence, receipts, and a timeline of events. 2. **Notify the Landlord in Writing** – Send a certified letter or email with a read receipt. 3. **Check Local Ordinances** – Some cities (e.g., Austin, Dallas, Houston) have additional tenant protections. 4. **File a Complaint** – If the issue isn’t resolved, file with TDHCA, HUD, or TCHR. 5. **Seek Legal Advice** – Contact a local tenant‑rights group or a licensed attorney. --- #### Useful Resources | Resource | What It Offers | |----------|----------------| | **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)** | Information on landlord‑tenant laws, complaint filing, and housing assistance. | | **U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)** | Federal fair‑housing enforcement. | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR)** | Handles discrimination complaints. | | **Local Tenant‑Rights Organizations** | Free or low‑cost legal clinics, mediation services. | | **Texas Property Code** | Full statutory text (available online). | --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, fair treatment, and due process in disputes. Keep records, communicate in writing, and know where to turn for help if your landlord violates your rights.
